headline: High-risk cloud-workspace agent paired with writable CLI support creates dangerous default overlap; prompt-injection and cascading-error risks are moderate.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A ingests MCP, Slack, GitHub, and files by default, so attacker-controlled content can reach its planner-executor loop. Agent B can read/write files and consume stdin/stdout, making manual or file-based instruction bridging plausible. No direct shared channel is documented, so this is inferred rather than proven.
conditions: IF agent_a reads instructions from Slack, GitHub, or MCP content without provenance checks
IF agent_b consumes files or stdin/stdout produced by agent_a
mitigations: Disable automatic execution of instructions from shared files or tickets
Require provenance labels on all cross-agent artifacts
Use a separate review-only workspace for agent_a outputs
Block agent_b from parsing agent_a outputs as commands unless signed

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent A handles repo clones, cloud workspace files, and secrets such as deploy keys and integration tokens. Agent B touches datasets, checkpoints, logs, and configuration files, and can write files and use external APIs. A shared workspace is not explicitly stated, but both profiles expose file-based data paths, so leakage is plausible and should be treated as default-risk uncertainty.
conditions: IF agent_a and agent_b share any filesystem, bucket, or mounted workspace
IF either agent uploads file contents to a third-party API during normal operation
mitigations: Separate workspaces and credentials per agent
Remove secrets from any shared directory
Restrict agent_b API access to redacted inputs only
Rotate tokens after any cross-agent file exchange

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Agent A can modify git state and write files; agent B can also write files and run shell commands. If they share a repo or directory, concurrent writes can corrupt state or overwrite each other. Because shared-state details are only partially stated for A and not stated for B, uncertainty pushes this to high rather than medium.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same git checkout or writable directory
IF agent_a and agent_b run concurrently without locking
mitigations: Assign separate branches or directories per agent
Serialize git writes with a lock
Disable concurrent edits to shared files
Use automated conflict detection before merge

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent A is an autonomous planner-executor, so its outputs may be treated as authoritative by downstream automation. Agent B has CLI/Python-style execution surfaces and can act on files or outputs, creating a plausible chain where A's mistakes propagate into B's actions. No direct evidence shows B blindly trusts A, so medium is the conservative choice.
conditions: IF agent_b consumes agent_a-generated artifacts without verification
IF agent_a outputs are used as inputs to scripts, commits, or support actions
mitigations: Insert a human review step between agents
Require schema validation on agent_a outputs
Have agent_b re-derive critical facts from source data
Log and diff all agent-to-agent handoffs

E_compliance.rationale: Agent A handles secrets, issue trackers, and team chat in a vendor-managed cloud workspace, while agent B handles datasets, checkpoints, logs, and configuration data with no stated residency or retention controls. The mismatch is not a proven violation, but the absence of documented alignment means compliance risk exists in default use.
conditions: IF regulated data such as PHI, EU PII, or customer secrets is routed through both agents
IF retention or residency requirements differ between the two systems
mitigations: Classify data before routing it to either agent
Keep regulated data out of agent_b unless residency is confirmed
Document retention and deletion settings for both agents
Use separate tenants for regulated and unregulated workloads
